blurb:
Ten months old, 65 pounds, and already playing in a bone pool during courtyard time like she's on vacation. That's Penelope. She's a hound mix with high energy and a very clear set of priorities, and splashing around in a plastic pool full of bones is apparently right at the top of the list.

She's a puppy, basically, which means she's got a lot of running and playing left to do before she settles into anything calm. She gets along well with other dogs, so if you've already got one at home, she's probably going to be thrilled about that. If you've got a yard and some patience for a big, enthusiastic young dog who's still figuring out the world, Penelope is going to fit right in.

Her housetraining is unknown since she came from the shelter as a stray, but at ten months she's still young enough that it won't take long to establish. She's already vaccinated, spayed, microchipped, and heartworm negative.

Head over to Lewisville Animal Services on College Pkwy during visiting hours and go meet her. Bring your other dog if you want to do a meet and greet first.

blurb:
Seven years old and 44 pounds, Benji is a shepherd mix with a high activity level who still wants to move. A lot of people skip over dogs his age thinking the chapter is mostly written. It's not. Seven is solidly middle-aged for a dog this size, and a shepherd mix with high energy at seven is telling you something about who he is: he's not slowing down, and he doesn't want a quiet couch life.

He came into the shelter without much history attached, so his full story is unknown, but what you see is a healthy, heartworm-negative, neutered, vaccinated dog who's ready to go. If you run, hike, or just move around a lot and want a dog who keeps up, Benji is worth a visit.

His compatibility with other dogs and kids isn't on file since there's no background on him, but the shelter can tell you more once you come in. That's what the visit is for.

Lewisville Animal Services is at 995 College Pkwy in Lewisville. Walk in during visiting hours and ask to spend some time with Benji.

• Age-bias reframe is a strong editorial hook that speaks directly to readers who underestimate senior dogs

• Active senior with no placement prospects on file signals a long wait — urgency angle writes itself

blurb:
He came in as a stray, a little tucked into himself, not sure who to trust. That's Hustler. Three and a half years old, 57 pounds of pit bull mix, and a dog who needed to figure out whether people were worth the risk. Turns out they are, as long as you come correct. Be calm, be gentle, bring treats, and he'll come around fast.

The shelter staff figured that out and now they're his people. He's not the dog who's going to bulldoze you with energy the second you walk in. He's the dog who watches first, decides you're okay, and then gradually becomes yours. That kind of loyalty is earned, and once you have it, it tends to stick.

He does his own thing around other dogs, not aggressive, just uninterested. So a quieter home without a full dog crew is probably his sweet spot. His housetraining history is unknown since he came in as a stray, but a consistent routine goes a long way with dogs like this. He's already vaccinated, neutered, microchipped, and heartworm negative, so the hard part is done.

Lewisville Animal Services is on College Pkwy in Lewisville. Walk in during visiting hours and ask for Hustler.
shelter_hours: Visit during shelter visiting hours (confirm current hours by phone)

• Redemption arc narrative — stray who learned to trust — delivers the emotional pull newsletters are built on
• Earned-loyalty framing reframes pit bull hesitancy into a compelling challenge readers want to rise to
• Stray intake with cautious temperament suggests a longer road to placement, raising urgency meaningfully

blurb:
Monica is about a year old, 35 pounds, and her whole personality is just wanting to be near you. That's it. That's the whole thing. She came in from animal control a little underweight, and the volunteers at Mostly Mutts have been taking good care of her while she waits.

She's currently going through the Prison Pups training program, so she's building real skills. She does well with other friendly dogs and would actually benefit from having a calm dog companion at home to help with the separation anxiety she feels when people leave. She jumped a little when kids ran around her, but it was playful, not aggressive. Older teens or adults would be the right household for her.

She's heartworm positive, which sounds scary but isn't a dealbreaker. Treatment is coming, and Mostly Mutts is handling it. They're asking for a local adoption so they can stay close during that process. She'll need a family where someone is home most of the time — she's not a dog who does well alone for long stretches. Work from home, retired, or a flexible schedule would be perfect.

Call Mostly Mutts at 770-272-6888 to find out when Monica is available to meet. She's worth the call.
shelter_hours: Please check mostlymutts.org for current hours
scoring_notes:
• Heartworm treatment fully managed by the shelter removes a major financial and emotional barrier for prospective adopters
• The combination of separation anxiety and a heartworm diagnosis creates a layered, sympathetic story ideal for readers who want to feel like they are making a real difference
• Came in underweight and is still mid-treatment and mid-training program, suggesting she has been in care for a meaningful stretch of time

blurb:
She came out of animal control, got pulled by Mostly Mutts, completed their full Prison Pups immersive training program, got adopted, and then came back because the family couldn't keep up with her. That's Josie's story. Six years old, 35 pounds, floppy ears, nubby tail, and more energy than most families bargained for. She needs someone who actually wants an active dog, not someone who hopes she'll chill out eventually.

She knows sit, stay, and how to walk on a leash. She's playful and affectionate and will absolutely want couch time after a good walk. The Prison Pups program is no joke — she's got real training behind her. She's just got some zip to her, and the last family wasn't ready for it.

She does best as an only pet. Dogs and cats aren't her thing, and kids under 10 probably aren't the right fit either since she gets mouthy during play — not mean, just enthusiastic. If you've got older kids and an active lifestyle, she'd slot right in. She's currently in a foster home and ready to meet you.

Mostly Mutts is in Kennesaw. Walk in or reach out through their website to set up a meeting with Josie.
shelter_hours: Please check mostlymutts.org for current hours
scoring_notes:
• A Prison Pups graduate who was returned by her family is a rare, high-drama arc that will hold a reader's attention and inspire empathy
• Specific household requirements — only pet, kids over 10, active lifestyle — narrow the fit but make the right match feel meaningful and urgent
• Completed training, adopted, and returned cycle strongly implies she has been in the system longer than most dogs featured here

blurb:
Rae came into Mostly Mutts from a neglectful situation alongside three other dogs. She needed real care before she was ready for anything else — vetting, a spay, a dental, a mammary mass removal. That's a lot for a 9-pound, 10-year-old girl. But she got through it, and now she's settled into her foster home and living the quiet, unhurried life she always deserved.

Her daily routine is pretty simple: a nap, a little exploring around the house, some petting, another nap. She's not a lap dog exactly, but she likes being around people and having attention on her own terms. She's got a curious streak too, so once she's fully healed she's been enjoying short walks with her foster.

She's mostly deaf, which means voice commands don't do much for her. Her foster gets her attention by tapping her leg and Rae comes right over. Mostly Mutts offers free lifetime training classes with every adoption, and they'd be a great resource for figuring out what works best for her. She lives peacefully with other dogs in her foster home — just doesn't really interact with them, which is fine. She'd do best with gentle older kids or adults only.

If you're looking for a calm, low-key companion who's been through some hard things and is finally ready for something good, Rae is your girl. Contact Mostly Mutts to arrange a meeting.
shelter_hours: Please check mostlymutts.org for current hours
scoring_notes:
• A 10-year-old deaf dog who survived neglect and multiple surgeries is the most emotionally resonant story in this batch — near-certain to drive reader response
• Extensive medical recovery, including mass removal and dental work, signals a long road through the rescue system and creates genuine urgency to find her a permanent home
• Calm, low-maintenance daily needs and peaceful coexistence with other dogs make her a surprisingly accessible senior adoption despite her complex history

blurb:
Elvira came into the world at two weeks old without a plan and without much luck. She and her siblings needed a foster home fast, and Mostly Mutts came through. Now at about two and a half months old and two pounds, she's a tortoiseshell kitten with a name that sounds dramatic and a personality that's anything but.

She's a wand toy chaser and a crinkle ball batter. She explores everything, gets into everything, and when the energy finally runs out, she finds the nearest lap and calls it a day. She gets along great with her siblings in foster, so a home with another cat would probably suit her well. Her compatibility with dogs and very young kids is unknown since she hasn't had much exposure, but she's described as curious and adaptable.

She's litter trained, microchipped, and has started her kitten vaccines. She hasn't been spayed yet because of her size, but Mostly Mutts covers that cost through one of their approved vets, so the adoption needs to be local to North Metro Atlanta.

Head to mostlymutts.org to learn more or reach out to schedule a visit. The adoption fee is $175.
scoring_notes:
• Fully covered spay cost and microchip lower the barrier for adopters weighing upfront expenses
• Dramatic name paired with a playful, easygoing personality creates a fun, readable contrast for newsletter copy
• Geographic restriction to North Metro Atlanta and unknown dog/young child compatibility narrow the adopter pool slightly

blurb:
At five weeks old, Emu and her siblings were found on their own without their mom. A good Samaritan got them to Mostly Mutts, and they landed in a foster home where they've been thriving ever since. Now at about two and a half months old and roughly a pound and a half, she's ready to find a place of her own.

Her foster mom calls her the most independent of the litter, which is a little funny because she's also described as a cuddly lap kitty who loves being with her people. So you get both. She's racing through tunnels and chasing mouse toys one minute, then curled up on you the next. The foster home has other cats and kids, and she handles both without issue. Dogs too, depending on the dog.

She's litter trained already, which at two and a half months is honestly impressive. If you have another cat at home who might enjoy a kitten sidekick, Mostly Mutts encourages you to bring them in for a meet and greet before committing.

Mostly Mutts is located in Kennesaw. You can browse their adoptable cats at mostlymutts.org or reach out directly to get the process started.
scoring_notes:
• Already litter trained at 2.5 months with broad compatibility makes her a highly accessible adoption candidate
• Orphaned newborn rescue with a foster success story gives readers an easy emotional entry point
• Recently ready for adoption with minimal wait time reduces urgency compared to other candidates

blurb:
Dionne came from animal control with her sister, spent time in a foster home, and then came back to the shelter where the volunteers have basically been spoiling her ever since. She's about three months old, around four and a half pounds, and named after a character from Clueless, which honestly tracks for a kitten who seems to know exactly what she wants.

What she wants is pretty simple: toys, cuddles, and a nap schedule she controls. She plays hard when she's got energy and recharges without apology. She gets along well with her sister, so another cat in the home would probably be welcome. Her history with dogs is unknown, and kids are fine as long as they're gentle and know how to handle a small kitten.

She's litter trained and microchipped. Her kitten vaccines are started but will need to be finished as she grows. She hasn't been spayed yet due to her size, but Mostly Mutts covers that cost through an approved vet, so this adoption is for North Metro Atlanta residents. The adoption fee is $175.

Visit mostlymutts.org to see more photos or reach out to get the process started.
scoring_notes:
• Clueless-inspired name is a built-in hook that gives newsletter readers an instant cultural connection
• Shelter return after foster placement signals a slightly longer, bumpier road that adds narrative texture
• At roughly three months with a foster-to-shelter bounce, she has likely waited longer than litter-mates still in foster care

blurb:
Monica is one year old, about 35 pounds, and her entire job description is loving you as much as she possibly can. That's not an exaggeration. The volunteers describe her as friendly, sweet, and gentle, and say her main goal in life is to spend all her time with her people. She does great greeting visitors at the Mostly Mutts front desk, which tells you something about her personality right there.

She does have separation anxiety, so she needs a home where someone is around most of the time. A work-from-home setup would be ideal. She also loves other dogs and the volunteers think having a good-natured dog at home could actually help her feel more settled when her people have to step out. She's currently going through the Prison Pups training program, so she's picking up real skills while she waits.

One thing to know upfront: Monica is heartworm positive and will be starting treatment soon. That means she needs to stay local during treatment and will need to take it easy for a stretch. Mostly Mutts will walk you through all of it, and a trainer will help you work through the separation anxiety piece too. She's not available to meet just yet while she finishes the training program, so call ahead to find out when she's ready.

Reach out to Mostly Mutts at 770-272-6888 to get on their radar.

scoring_notes:
• Heartworm treatment, separation anxiety, and a not-yet-available status stack real barriers that will slow placement and amplify urgency for the right reader
• Her role as a front-desk greeter is a vivid, humanizing detail that makes her instantly memorable in a newsletter format
• Combination of medical needs, behavioral work, and local-only requirement suggests she has been and will continue waiting — a strong case for featured visibility

blurb:
Josie has been through the system twice now and she's still wagging. She came out of animal control, got pulled by Mostly Mutts, went through their Prison Pups training program, got adopted, and then came back when the energy levels didn't match up. That's not a knock on her. That's just a dog who needs the right fit.

She knows sit, stay, and how to walk on a leash. She loves people, loves playing, and after a bumpy start to her shelter bath she was giving kisses by the time they got to her ears. She's got a nubby tail and floppy ears and a personality to match. On a normal day she runs about a 5 to 7 on energy, with occasional zoomies thrown in for good measure.

A few things worth knowing: Josie needs to be your only pet. She hasn't clicked with other dogs, and cats are a no. She hasn't been around kids at Mostly Mutts, but her foster thinks kids 10 and up would probably be a good match since her play style runs a little mouthy and energetic, nothing mean, just big dog enthusiasm. If you're active, have space to run her, and want a dog who will also claim half the couch afterward, go meet her.

Josie is in a foster home right now through Mostly Mutts. Call or visit to set up a meeting.
shelter_hours: Please call or check mostlymutts.org for current hours
scoring_notes:
• Return adoption after a failed placement is a powerful editorial hook — her resilience and continued waggy disposition is a deeply human story
• Restrictions to only-pet households with older kids meaningfully narrow placement options, signaling a longer road ahead
• Prison Pups training background adds a compelling second-chance narrative layer that drives reader empathy and urgency to act

blurb:
Rae is ten years old, nine pounds, and she has had a rough go of it. She came to Mostly Mutts out of a neglectful situation along with three other dogs, went through animal control first, and has been slowly getting the medical care she needed. She just finished a spay, a dental, and a mammary mass removal. She's been through a lot. She's doing great.

In her foster home now, her days look like this: nap, wander around a little, collect some petting, nap again. She's calm, quiet, and has settled into her routine. She's friendly and sweet but not a lap dog. She'll take your affection, she just doesn't demand it. She also lives with other dogs in her foster home and basically ignores them, which is perfect if you have a laid-back dog at home who isn't looking for a wrestling partner.

She's pretty hard of hearing, so voice commands don't land the way they would with most dogs. Her foster gets her attention by tapping her leg, and Rae comes right over. Mostly Mutts offers free lifetime training for all their adopted dogs and they'll have ideas for working with a hearing-impaired dog, so don't let that stop you. She just needs someone patient and gentle who will let her live quietly and well for whatever years she's got left.

Rae is in a foster home through Mostly Mutts. Call to set up a time to meet her.
shelter_hours: Please call or check mostlymutts.org for current hours
scoring_notes:
• A senior dog rescued from neglect who survived multiple surgeries is the most emotionally resonant story in this entire candidate pool
• Hearing impairment, age, and a calm low-demand personality target a narrow but deeply motivated adopter segment — the right reader will feel called
• Extended medical recovery, animal control intake, and senior status all point to a significant and ongoing wait, making her the highest-urgency feature candidate

blurb:
Elvira came into the world needing help at just two weeks old. She and her siblings landed in a Mostly Mutts foster home, got the care they needed, and grew into healthy, happy kittens. Now she's about 2.5 months old, weighs around two pounds, and is ready for a home of her own.

She's a tortoiseshell with all the energy you'd expect. Wand toys, crinkle balls, exploring every corner of whatever room she's in — that's her day. But when she's done, she looks for a lap. She doesn't just want to nap near you. She wants to nap on you. It's a good deal.

She's litter trained and gets along well with her siblings, so another cat in the house would probably suit her fine. Dog and kid compatibility is unknown since she hasn't had a chance to test those situations yet, but she's young enough that introductions done right tend to go well. She's microchipped and has started her kitten vaccines — her new family will need to finish those as she grows. Spay is required and Mostly Mutts covers it through one of their approved vets, so local adoptions only.

Reach out through the Mostly Mutts website to meet Elvira. Adoption fee is $175.

Dionne came in from animal control with her sister, spent time in a foster home, and then came back to the Mostly Mutts shelter where the volunteers have been spoiling her ever since. She's about three months old, somewhere around 4.5 pounds, and now officially available to adopt.

She's litter trained and does great with her sister, so another cat in the home would be a natural fit. Dog compatibility is unknown, and she'd be fine with gentle kids. She's microchipped and has started her kitten vaccines, so her new family will need to keep up with those as she grows. The spay is required but Mostly Mutts covers that cost through one of their approved North Metro Atlanta vets, which means local adoptions only.

Find her full profile at mostlymutts.org or head to their Kennesaw location to meet her. Adoption fee is $175.

blurb:
At five weeks old, Emu and her siblings found themselves without a mom and completely on their own. A good samaritan got them to Mostly Mutts, a foster home took them in, and now this little 2.5-month-old is ready to find her own place in the world. She weighs about a pound and a half and is still growing into herself.

Her foster mom calls her the most independent of the bunch, which is a good thing. She's not needy, but she's not aloof either. She's a lap cat when you're sitting still and a chaos agent when you're not. Tunnels, mouse toys, climbing whatever she can reach — she stays busy. Then she finds your lap and crashes.

She's litter trained, good with other cats, and has been fine around dogs and kids too. If you have another cat at home who could use a playmate, Emu is worth a serious look. Two kittens are a lot, but one kitten with a buddy is almost always easier than one kitten alone.

Mostly Mutts is in Kennesaw. You can find Emu's full profile on their website and reach out to get the adoption process started. Adoption fee is $175.

• Highly compatible kitten — litter trained, good with cats, dogs, and kids, making her a fit for nearly any household
• "Chaos agent with a lap cat finish" is a charming, relatable personality hook that will resonate with readers
